title: Crown and Choir
premise: Marguerite Nakamura, a bone-carver who hears the dead through the relics he carves, has lived his whole life in the Hollow Valley, a sanctuary where magic cannot follow. When the old gods resume answering prayers, their voices bleed into his carvings, and he learns the covenant binding gods and mortals was shattered thirteen years ago — by his own mother, the valley's founder. Dragged beyond the valley's edge as the moon nears its thirteenth turn, Marguerite must gather the scattered fragments of the broken covenant and decide whether to restore it whole or rewrite it, knowing restoration means silencing the dead he loves and rewriting means unleashing unbound gods. In the end he reforges the covenant with a clause of his own: memory shared between realms, so neither gods nor mortals can again rule through forgetting — at the cost of his own gift, leaving him deaf to the dead but finally able to hear the living.
about_author: Jude Nakamura spent a decade restoring liturgical instruments in coastal monasteries before turning to fiction, a trade that taught him how objects hold the prayers of their handlers. Crown and Choir is his second novel, following the quietly acclaimed The Salt Reliquary.

chapters.title: The Valley That Forgets
chapters.summary: POV Marguerite. In the Hollow Valley, Marguerite carves a memorial bone for a grieving widow and hears her dead husband's last words — routine work, until the voice continues after the carving is finished, begging him to leave the valley. He dismisses it as fatigue, but that night every finished piece in his workshop whispers at once. Emotional beat: unease beneath domestic calm.

chapters.title: Thirteen Bells
chapters.summary: POV Marguerite. The old god Vessia answers a child's prayer publicly for the first time in living memory, and pilgrims flood the valley seeking sanctuary from miracles. Marguerite's aunt Serah reveals fragments of a family secret: his mother didn't die thirteen years ago; she left, and the valley's magic-dead border was her doing. Emotional beat: betrayal cracking open a sheltered life.

chapters.title: What the Border Keeps Out
chapters.summary: POV Marguerite. A wounded god-touched stranger, Ilex, collapses at the valley's edge, pursued by zealots who believe answered prayers are an invasion. Saving him means carrying him across the border — where Marguerite's hearing sharpens agonizingly and he hears his mother's voice among the dead. Emotional beat: grief weaponized into resolve.

chapters.title: The Choir of Small Gods
chapters.summary: POV Ilex. Beyond the valley, Ilex guides Marguerite through a countryside where minor gods have gone drunk on new power, demanding worship through fear. They discover a fragment of the shattered covenant inscribed on a church bell, singing a counter-melody to the gods' chorus. Emotional beat: wonder curdling into dread at what power does to the small.

chapters.title: Bone and Bell
chapters.summary: POV Marguerite. Zealots capture them; their leader, Prelate Ossian, turns out to be a former friend of Marguerite's mother who believes the covenant must stay broken so mortals remain free. He offers Marguerite a place at his side. Marguerite escapes with the bell-fragment but steals Ossian's ledger of the covenant's original terms. Emotional beat: loyalty tested against truth.

chapters.title: My Mother's Handwriting
chapters.summary: POV Marguerite. The ledger reveals Marguerite's mother broke the covenant deliberately to trap something inside it — not to free mortals, but to imprison a starving god she had loved. Her voice, carried in a carved keepsake Marguerite bears, confesses she used her son's unborn gift as the seal. Emotional beat: devastating recognition that he was always part of the design.

chapters.title: The Thirteenth Turn Begins
chapters.summary: POV Ilex. With the moon entering its final turn, unbound gods begin consuming mortal memories to sustain themselves; villages forget their own names. Ilex, revealed as a demoted god himself, sacrifices his remaining divinity to shield one village, becoming fully mortal. Emotional beat: self-erasure as an act of love and proof power can be refused.

chapters.title: Where the Covenant Was Broken
chapters.summary: POV Marguerite. At the ruin where his mother shattered the covenant, Marguerite finds her waiting — half-god now, sustained by the imprisoned deity, offering to restore everything if he takes her place as the seal. The dead he has heard all his life arrive as witnesses, testifying to both her mercy and her theft. Emotional beat: confrontation with the parent who made him an instrument.

chapters.title: A New Verse
chapters.summary: POV Marguerite. Climax. Refusing both restoration and his mother's bargain, Marguerite carves the covenant anew — into his own bones — adding the clause of shared memory between realms. The starving god is freed into remembrance rather than imprisonment; his mother dissolves into the choir she tried to silence. The moon completes its thirteenth turn over a world holding its breath. Emotional beat: sacrifice transmuted into authorship.

chapters.title: The Quiet After Singing
chapters.summary: POV Marguerite. Deaf to the dead, Marguerite returns to the valley, which now lets magic pass gently through it. He carves a final bone for the widow from chapter one — and cannot hear the answer, but the widow can, and tells him what her husband said. Gods and mortals begin meeting as neighbors. Emotional beat: bittersweet peace; loss exchanged for connection.
